e.etymology: A spelling of Hayley with the -leigh ending. Hayley is an English surname from a place name: Old English heg, 'hay', and leah, 'clearing, meadow'.
Spanish and Italian form of Abelard, known from the 12th-century French philosopher Peter Abelard, lover of Heloise. It is usually traced to Germanic Adalhard, 'noble' plus 'hardy, strong'.
An African American coinage joining Trey, a nickname for a third-generation namesake from the word for three, to the -von ending of Devon and Javon. Also spelled Trayvon.

assoc.t: sounds like Trayvon Martin, teen killed in Florida in 2012

e.etymology: From the English word and title judge, from Old French juge and Latin iudex. Nineteenth-century American parents gave titles such as Judge, Major and General as first names; it is also an occupational surname.
namesakes: Judge Reinhold (actor in Beverly Hills Cop)

assoc.t: the courtroom title, as in Judge Judy

e.note: Reads as a title, so a boy named Judge Smith may be taken for an actual judge on paper.

e.etymology: The French form of Elijah, Hebrew Eliyahu, 'my God is Yahweh', and a short form of Eliezer. It is common among French speakers and Lebanese Christians; for girls it is also a spelling of Ellie.
namesakes: Elie Wiesel (Holocaust survivor and author of Night)

e.meaning: the last letter of the Greek alphabet; the end
e.etymology: The last letter of the Greek alphabet, literally o mega, 'great O'. In Revelation God says 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end', and the name was sometimes given to a last-born child.

assoc.t: Omega, the Swiss luxury watch maker
omega-3 fatty acids, as in fish oil
Greek letter in fraternity and sorority names

e.etymology: Spanish form of Briseis, Achilles' captive in the Iliad, whose Greek name means 'daughter of Briseus'. Medieval romances told her story under the name Briseida, the model for Chaucer's and Shakespeare's Cressida.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese name from Latin Silvana, the feminine of Silvanus, the Roman god of woods and fields, from silva, 'forest'.
In English a surname and title for the older of two people of the same name, from Old English eldra, 'older'. Elder is also an established first name in Central America, Colombia and Brazil.

assoc.t: elder, a church office and Latter-day Saint missionary title
the elder tree, source of elderberries

e.etymology: A respelling of Micah, the Hebrew prophet whose book is in the Old Testament. Micah is a short form of Mikhayahu, 'who is like Yahweh?'.
A spelling of Alaina, which is variously a feminine of Alan and a variant of Elaine and Helen. Some families use it for Alina instead.
Yiddish form of Yehudis, the Hebrew name Judith, 'woman of Judea' or 'Jewish woman'. It is used in Hasidic Jewish communities.
Yiddish for 'pearl', cognate with German Perle. A traditional Ashkenazi girls' name, now used mainly in Hasidic communities; Perl and Pearl are the same name.
Finnish everyday form of Mikael (Michael), from Hebrew Mikha'el, 'who is like God?', in use since the Middle Ages.
English surname from places named Haddon, Old English haeth, 'heath', and dun, 'hill'. As the middle name of Victorian Baptist preacher Charles Haddon Spurgeon, it is sometimes chosen in his honor.
Spanish for 'kings', referring to the Three Kings of Epiphany, los Reyes Magos. It began as a devotional name, often for children born around January 6, and is also a common Spanish surname.

e.meaning: dweller on land cleared by fire
e.etymology: German surname for someone living on land cleared by burning, from Brand, 'fire'. As a first name it sits beside Brant and Brent.

In English from Maida, the Calabrian town where Britain won an 1806 battle, taken up as a girls' name and heard as a form of maid. Maida is also used in Bosnia, linked to Arabic ma'ida, 'table', the title of a Quran chapter.

assoc.t: maida, the refined white flour of Indian cooking

e.etymology: From the same root as Angela: Greek angelos, 'messenger, angel'. Angeli is the Italian word for angels and is also used as a short form of Angelica and Angelina, notably in the Philippines.
A spelling of Evelyn with a French-style ending. Evelyn began as an English surname from the Norman girls' name Aveline, a pet form of Germanic Avila, and was first given to boys.

Used in Spanish-speaking American families, peaking in the early 2000s, in many spellings such as Naidelyn and Neidelyn. Its source is not established; it follows the sound of Nayeli, Madelyn and Jocelyn.
A respelling of the word tough, used as a nickname in rodeo country. Champion bull rider Tuff Hedeman, portrayed in the 1994 film 8 Seconds, made it familiar, and it is now given as a first name.

assoc.t: tuff, current youth slang for cool or impressive
tuff, rock formed from volcanic ash

e.etymology: A short form of Llywelyn, the name of medieval Welsh princes, from a Celtic compound of the god names Lugus and Belenus, long linked to llew, 'lion'. The 2013 film Inside Llewyn Davis made this spelling known.

assoc.t: folk singer of the Coen brothers' Inside Llewyn Davis

e.etymology: A recent elaboration of Ava with the -ana ending of Ariana and Aviana; it also echoes Havana and Ivana.
From Sanskrit vayu, 'wind, air'. Vayu is the Hindu god of the wind, father of Hanuman and of Bhima, and the word names the vital breath in yoga teaching.
Short form of Patricia, the feminine of Latin patricius, 'nobleman, patrician'. A separate Indian name Trisha comes from Sanskrit trsha, 'thirst, longing'.
A pet form of Ronald, the Scottish form of Old Norse Rögnvaldr, from regin, counsel, and valdr, ruler. Ronnie is the more common American spelling; Ronny is usual in Scandinavia and Germany.
namesakes: Ronny Chieng (comedian and Daily Show correspondent)
Ronny Cox (actor in Deliverance and RoboCop)

e.etymology: An English and Welsh surname meaning son of William, itself from Germanic wil, will, and helm, helmet. It is among the most common surnames in the US and is occasionally given as a first name.

assoc.t: one of the three most common surnames in the US
Williams, the British Formula One racing team

e.note: Reads as a surname or as a slip for William, so expect it to be corrected often.

e.etymology: A spelling of Ty, the short form of Tyler, Tyrone and Tyson. Tye is also an English surname, from Middle English tye, a village green or enclosed pasture.
namesakes: Tye Sheridan (actor in Ready Player One and the X-Men films)

e.etymology: The feminine of Simon in Italian and many Central and Eastern European languages. Simon is the Greek form of Hebrew Shimon, he has heard.
namesakes: Simona Halep (Romanian tennis player, Wimbledon and French Open champion)

e.etymology: An African American coinage of the later 20th century, built on Javon with the -te ending of Dante and Deonte.
A modern American spelling of Kaliyah, one of the many -iyah names that followed Aaliyah in the 2000s. The Kh- echoes Arabic-style names such as Khalil and Khadijah.
